note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · SEE THE FEMALE WEB
tiles.details: Start with true Bob Harms, source-labelled Texas bluegrass PISTILLATE heads: panel 0 is the full female panicle; panel 1 shows the web-like pale hairs on green attached spikelets; panel 3 contains separately displayed female reproductive units with a real source scale. The web comes from hairs around the lemma callus, NOT from stigmas or the leaves. Many spiderweb-like strands are visible in the photos, but their exact individual insertion points and measured lengths are not independently arrow-confirmed. This is useful photo evidence, NOT by itself evidence of a Hays-collected voucher.
tiles.short: Silky cobwebs surround the female spikelets
tiles.status: ACTUAL FEMALE HEAD/WEB PHOTOGRAPHED — fine insertion still unresolved

tiles.heading: 02 · FIND THE TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: The true P. arachnifera source-photo triptych (panel 6) shows green sheath, the attached blade and pointed upright PALE LIGULE membrane near their inner junction; its one existing arrow is on visible membrane tissue. A Williamson County specimen treatment reports a smooth, milky-translucent 0.5–2 mm membranous ligule; the broader FNA treatment uses about 1–4 mm. Those are PUBLISHED values, not measurements made from this archived image. The pale membrane is NOT an awn, and both annual bluegrass and Kentucky bluegrass may also have membranous ligules. The P. annua collar shown in panel 9 is a different species.
tiles.short: Milky membrane between blade and sheath, not an awn
tiles.status: TRUE SPECIES-MATCHED LIGULE PHOTO VISIBLE; physical 1-mm membrane calibration pending

tiles.heading: 03 · CHECK THE SEEDHEAD AND SEX
tiles.details: The adult P. arachnifera female head in panel 0 has ascending branches; younger female units in panel 1 are densely webbed. Dry, later-stage female panicle panel 5 may show less conspicuous webbing. Texas bluegrass is dioecious, so separate individual plants bear staminate (male) or pistillate (female) flowers. A genuine male image must show a source-verified plant with functional anthers and a dissected male floret; smoothness alone is insufficient, because male florets can have sparse basal hairs, and old female webs can be worn away. Panel 4 is a source-linked FEMALE dried head, NOT a male.
tiles.short: Female panicles can be webby; male panicles not yet documented
tiles.status: FEMALE PHOTOS VERIFIED; ACTUAL MALE FLOWER/ANTHER PHOTOS MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · LIFT AND TRACE RHIZOMES
tiles.details: Texas bluegrass spreads through slender BELOW-GROUND rhizomes and produces fibrous adventitious roots; this cannot be diagnosed from the flower pictures. The local Williamson County treatment describes horizontal rhizomes commonly about 2 cm beneath the soil, to about 8 cm long and 0.7–1 mm wide. These values are from literature, NOT photographed measurements. On a legitimately sampled plant, lift soil to trace an INTACT horizontal rhizome from one rooted leafy ramet to another; photograph its nodes, bud/sheath, attached roots and a centimeter ruler without severing the connection. A dense rootless aboveground clump proves nothing about a rhizome.
tiles.short: Perennial slender underground connections, not simply dense tillers
tiles.status: CRITICAL PHOTO GAP — connected rhizome with two living rooted shoots not photographed

tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT A FEMALE AND A MALE
tiles.details: The separated, author-identified female reproductive units in panel 3 show real long silky strands beside individual bracts, but the photograph does not trace three independent callus webs or distinguish every lemma/glume boundary. Flora of North America describes female calluses as commonly 3-webbed with long (4–10 mm) plicate hairs; male calluses usually glabrous or sparsely webbed, though some can still have hairs. The needed matched set: source-verified female spikelet and male staminate spikelet, separately opened glumes/lemmas and sexual organs, each beside a physical 1-mm scale. Never infer functional sex from hair density alone.
tiles.short: Female three-web callus versus male sparse-web callus
tiles.status: PISTILLATE MICRO PHOTOS AVAILABLE; PAIRED STAMINATE DISSECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT OTHER POA
tiles.details: The annual-bluegrass P. annua comparisons in panels 7–9 show a real small whole flowering plant, boat-prow leaf tip and membranous ligule. These photos are explicitly NOT Texas bluegrass. P. annua is commonly annual, lacks connected perennial rhizomes and generally has bisexual flowers. Introduced Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) may be perennial AND rhizomatous, so only the rhizome/boat-tip combination is not enough; compare genuinely dioecious floral anatomy and marked female basal callus webbing. If male flower sex and underground connections cannot be independently established, teach the record as Poa sp. until resolved.
tiles.short: Boat-shaped leaf tip and ligule only prove you should check Poa
tiles.status: OTHER-SPECIES PHOTO COMPARISON PRESENT; RHIZOME AND MALE-FLORET CONFIRMATION PENDING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: TEXAS BLUEGRASS — native cool-season RHIZOMATOUS perennial and DIOECIOUS (female and male flowering plants separate). First see the source-photographed FEMALE spikelet basal cobwebs (Harms POAR-F2/FS), then the real MEMBRANOUS collar ligule (Harms POAR-L). Don't call a grass Texas bluegrass from a boat-shaped leaf tip or hairy-looking flowering head alone. The exact missing crew-confirmation photographs remain the MALE staminate floret and an intact underground RHIZOME linking rooted shoots; the iNaturalist flowering-stand image does not expose roots.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1 · Look at a source-vouchered adult flowering stand, then a REAL POAR-F PISTILLATE panicle; these original Harms photos are true Poa arachnifera female-source labels, not mere green head guesses.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The true P. arachnifera source-photo triptych (panel 6) shows green sheath, the attached blade and pointed upright PALE LIGULE membrane near their inner junction; its one existing arrow is on visible membrane tissue. A Williamson County specimen treatment reports a smooth, milky-translucent 0.5–2 mm membranous ligule; the broader FNA treatment uses about 1–4 mm. Those are PUBLISHED values, not measurements made from this archived image. The pale membrane is NOT an awn, and both annual bluegrass and Kentucky bluegrass may also have membranous ligules. The P. annua collar shown in panel 9 is a different species.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: The adult P. arachnifera female head in panel 0 has ascending branches; younger female units in panel 1 are densely webbed. Dry, later-stage female panicle panel 5 may show less conspicuous webbing. Texas bluegrass is dioecious, so separate individual plants bear staminate (male) or pistillate (female) flowers. A genuine male image must show a source-verified plant with functional anthers and a dissected male floret; smoothness alone is insufficient, because male florets can have sparse basal hairs, and old female webs can be worn away. Panel 4 is a source-linked FEMALE dried head, NOT a male.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Both P. annua and Texas bluegrass have a membranous ligule and boat-shaped blade tips, so neither clue identifies the native species. Compare reproductive SEX on individually collected florets and actual connected underground rhizomes on same-plant clumps. Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) can also be rhizomatous and may have some basal lemma hairs; its flowers are bisexual, so woolliness alone does not prove P. arachnifera.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: TEXAS BLUEGRASS: a creeping RHIZOMATOUS perennial with separate FEMALE and MALE plants. Female florets have actual long COBWEBBY BASAL HAIRS around the lemmas: see isolated true female spikelets in POAR-FS. White true MEMBRANE ligule in POAR-L is Poa GENUS support, not itself a species split.
safety_note: 2026-10-26 repository reconciliation: 8 existing media records include SIX physically archived Bob Harms female/collar JPEGs, ONE physically archived original iNaturalist flowering stand (CC BY-NC conditional), and ONE Bob Harms F4 external-only photo. Ten current teaching panels are SEVEN exact-species (six local + one external F4) and THREE different-species Poa annua comparisons. Bob Harms photographs are copyrighted; site science/education use with credit is noted, but prior collection-specific permission memo reviewed external-display-only uses for four DIFFERENT images, not local copying/adaptation here. Preserve archive and clear exact scope before public certification. No male, connected rhizome or local same-voucher lineage photographed. No new JPEG/arrows/site deployment claimed.
field_rule: Real PISTILLATE POAR-FS / F2 webbing is a useful evidence-backed target species photo; true Poa L membrane is genus-wide. Final species call needs attached/reviewed female floret with sexual morphology and independently documented connected rhizome and male reference.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
